lesson_title: The Wet Side, the Dry Side
hook_text: Two towns ninety kilometres apart. One gets about six times more rain. The reason is standing between them.
clip_script: Newlands, Cape Town: about one thousand five hundred millimetres of rain a year. Worcester, ninety kilometres away: about two hundred and fifty. Between them? Mountains. Wet air blows in from the ocean, hits the slopes and is forced up. As it climbs, it cools, clouds form, and rain pours on the windward side. The air crosses the top, already wrung out, and sinks down the other side, warming as it goes. Warm, dry air means no rain: a rain shadow. On the east coast the same thing happens: Durban on the coast gets about one thousand millimetres, while Mthatha inland, behind higher ground, gets about six hundred and fifty. And here is a bonus: in South Africa, slopes facing north catch the most sun.
visual_style: A whiteboard mountain cross-section with an arrow climbing the left side under a rain cloud, crossing the summit, and sliding down the right side into a cracked, dry valley.
pacing: A punchy number contrast, a smooth diagram build, then a quick bonus.
call_to_action: Watch the full lesson and draw your own rain shadow.
